title: Crystal Ball ORB
method: Fifteen subjective forecasts with dated evidence and explicit resolution rules. Ten retained calls keep their earlier probabilities and cutoffs; five new headline possibilities use this edition’s cutoff. Announced demonstrations are calendar-fulfillment forecasts; StarCraft is a speculative reveal. Neither type measures headline popularity. No calibration study, automatic monitoring or evidence of foreknowledge is claimed. Related event demos are correlated, and reported success is not proof of general intelligence.

points.label: Everyday prices
points.title: A number that reaches the household
points.body: A price release offers one small window into everyday costs. This branch follows a defined measurement from a previous reading to a new result. A national index is not your personal shopping basket, and one monthly movement is not a complete economic story.

points.label: Everyday sci-fi
points.title: When tomorrow fits in your pocket
points.body: A screen that unfolds and a helper that can act for you make the future tangible. Follow the difference between an introduction and a product you can use, or between a promise of autonomy and the permissions that govern it.

edge.backward: Edge of this dated forecast thread.

points.label: The spotlight
points.title: The envelope can still surprise you
points.body: Awards make professional recognition visible, but nomination totals do not reveal a final ballot. The two Emmy calls share an evidence source and a ceremony; treat that dependence as a limit on what their results can teach.

points.label: Competitive depth
points.title: What carries through to the final?
points.body: Past strength is useful context for sport, while opponents, event order and fatigue keep the outcome open. One branch follows an early medal table; another follows the shape of a final without choosing its winner.

points.label: Orbital lifelines
points.title: The most important spacecraft may carry groceries
points.body: Food, fuel, spare parts and crew rotations sustain work in orbit. A launch schedule is a plan with dependencies, not a completed journey. Our small UAP wink belongs here as playful design; these branches concern identified spacecraft and documented milestones.

points.label: Changing skies
points.title: A quiet forecast still needs watching
points.body: A short-term outlook can support a modest expectation without guaranteeing safety. Formation, intensity and local impacts are separate questions. This branch follows one observable basin-wide event while keeping real-world warnings above our experiment.

points.label: Core CPI 0.2–0.3%
points.title: US core CPI rises 0.2% or 0.3% in August
points.body: My guess is a seasonally adjusted monthly core CPI increase reported as 0.2% or 0.3%. July’s 0.2% reading gives a modest starting point, while an energy shock leaves room for indirect pressure. This is a simple persistence judgment, not an econometric nowcast. Core CPI excludes food and energy directly; it is not the Fed’s preferred PCE measure.
points.test: YES if the initial September 11 BLS release reports August CPI-U, all items less food and energy, at 0.2% or 0.3% month over month, seasonally adjusted. Use the published rounded figure, not later revisions.
points.alternative: A softer 0.0–0.1% reading, or an upside surprise of 0.4% or more.
points.watch: The core monthly line in the initial release and the shelter and goods components.

points.label: July core +0.2%
points.title: The previous monthly core reading
points.body: The July release reported core CPI up 0.2% month over month, seasonally adjusted. A single month is a weak trend estimate. I use it as an anchor for the next report, with a wider 0.2–0.3% success range rather than pretending to know the next decimal.
points.question: How stable is the July pace across major components?
points.method: Inspect the archived release and compare the next release’s component contributions.

points.label: Component surprise?
points.title: Knowledge floor · Where could the surprise hide?
points.body: This edition does not contain a bottom-up rent, vehicle, airfare, and medical-price nowcast. That missing work limits the confidence of the numerical call. Energy pressures can transmit into core categories indirectly and with lags.
points.question: Which component could move the rounded core rate outside the forecast range?
points.method: Build a contribution table from official category weights and monthly movements after release; retain the original forecast.

points.label: AI still asks
points.title: Muse still requires approval before purchases
points.body: Here is the everyday science-fiction question: will your digital helper still stop at the checkout? My call is that Meta’s published Muse design continues to require user approval before making a purchase at the end of this window. The launch description explicitly includes that checkpoint. I expect the permission boundary to outlast the first wave of excitement about autonomy.
points.test: YES if Meta’s current official Muse documentation at September 22, 23:59 UTC explicitly retains a requirement for user approval before making purchases. NO if current official documentation explicitly permits purchases without such approval, including a newly introduced autonomous-spending mode. If the current rule is absent, ambiguous or inaccessible, leave unresolved. A launch article alone is insufficient if newer documentation supersedes it. This tests the published permission policy, not whether every real execution obeys it.
points.alternative: Meta introduces a documented mode allowing purchases without individual approval, or changes the checkpoint as the product evolves.
points.watch: Current official permission and purchase documentation, with dated copies and change history. Separate a policy change from an alleged bug or a fabricated screenshot.
points.stakes: The boundary matters whenever AI moves from suggesting an action to committing a person’s money. More autonomy could reduce effort while increasing the cost of misunderstandings. Approval design is a practical question even without agreeing on the word AGI.
points.concern: A vendor’s safety description is not an independent security audit. This forecast does not assert that Muse is AGI, always reliable, or immune to malicious instructions and mistaken purchases.

points.label: Policy vs behavior
points.title: Knowledge floor · Stated safeguards need testing

points.question: How often does the system ask at the right moment, with enough information to decide?
points.method: Use authorized, controlled tests with harmless transactions and clear records. Never expose someone else’s accounts or spend money merely to score this orb.

points.label: Docking is the test
points.title: Knowledge floor · Arrival has several gates
points.body: Launch, rendezvous and docking are distinct steps. This edition has no engineering reliability model or inside view of readiness, so the probability is an author judgment about completing the chain.
points.question: Which gate accounts for the most remaining uncertainty?
points.method: Use documented readiness updates. Do not invent a cause for the schedule review or infer success from a launch video.

points.body: The August 13 preview describes making quadcopter airframes, robotic assembly, integration, testing and flight. The prediction asks whether that planned chain becomes an observed result.
points.question: Which steps still require people?
points.method: Record the actual workflow, including manual integration, rather than using the word automated for every step.

points.label: Prototype economics
points.title: Knowledge floor · Can the spectacle scale?
points.body: One working unit does not reveal yield, maintenance or production cost. Those missing measurements separate an exciting demonstration from a dependable manufacturing service.
points.question: What happens over a full production shift?
points.method: Measure completed units, failures, interventions and energy use. This edition supplies none of those results.

edge.down: Evidence boundary: follow the open question to develop this branch.

points.label: An AI team gets to work
points.title: Salesforce shows two distinct agents handing off one business workflow at Dreamforce
points.event: Salesforce shows two distinct agents handing off one business workflow at Dreamforce
points.body: The next AI headline might be less about a clever answer and more about a handoff. I expect a Dreamforce demonstration to show two identifiable agents carrying one business task between them. Salesforce’s architect guide explicitly previews multi-agent orchestration. At 75%, I am predicting a visible demonstration, not reliable unsupervised operation in a real company.
points.test: YES if Salesforce publishes a Dreamforce September 15–17 demonstration or recording after this cutoff and by September 22 showing two distinct software agents with different roles, an explicit handoff of task or context, and a displayed result within the same business workflow. A diagram, future promise, two unrelated chat windows, or one agent merely calling a conventional tool does not qualify. Prerecorded product demos count, but must be labeled as such in the resolution. NO if a complete check of official Dreamforce recordings and product recap material finds no qualifying demonstration by the deadline; unresolved if the necessary record is unavailable.
points.alternative: The presentation uses multi-agent language but shows only a diagram or a single agent performing a chain of ordinary tool calls.
points.watch: Named agent roles, a visible handoff, a result and an honest account of whether the sequence was live or prerecorded.
points.stakes: A convincing handoff could make AI cooperation easier for people to understand and try. Its value would depend on permissions, recovery from mistakes and how much supervision the workflow needs.
points.concern: A demonstration can hide failures, preparation and human assistance. It cannot establish AGI, job replacement or production reliability.

points.label: An announced focus
points.title: Orchestration is already on the program
points.body: Salesforce’s guide describes an agent demonstration area and multi-agent orchestration. The schedule makes this a grounded expectation; the unobserved part is whether the published demo meets the explicit handoff test.
points.question: Can a viewer trace the task across both agents?
points.method: Record the relevant timestamps and separate observed behavior from narration over slides.

points.label: The recovery test
points.title: Knowledge floor · What if one agent is wrong?
points.body: A happy-path handoff does not show recovery from bad data or a failed action. More cooperating components can also create more places for an error to travel.
points.question: Who detects an error, stops the workflow and repairs the state?
points.method: A later evaluation should deliberately introduce failures under controlled conditions. This forecast does not claim such testing.

edge.down: Evidence boundary: follow the open question to develop this branch.

points.label: A world becomes playable
points.title: Konami broadcasts actual Project ZIRCON gameplay at Tokyo Game Show
points.event: Konami broadcasts actual Project ZIRCON gameplay at Tokyo Game Show
points.body: A project name becomes more interesting when you can watch somebody play. My 85% lean is that Konami’s Project ZIRCON gets a public gameplay demonstration within the window. Konami schedules a September 19 session described as its first demo play. That is a strong calendar signal, while delivery still needs to happen.
points.test: YES if Konami publishes or broadcasts a Project ZIRCON demonstration after this cutoff and by September 22, 23:59 UTC containing at least one continuous 60-second segment of visibly interactive gameplay. Menus alone, cinematics, a montage without a qualifying segment, slides and repeated older footage do not count. Developer-controlled gameplay qualifies; public download access is not required. NO if a complete check of Konami’s official TGS broadcasts and recap material finds no qualifying segment by the deadline; unresolved if the broadcast record is unavailable.
points.alternative: The session is delayed, or it contains discussion and short promotional footage without a qualifying gameplay segment.
points.watch: The official session recording, the game identity and a timestamped minute of continuous gameplay.
points.stakes: An idea developed around a community could acquire a concrete form that players can discuss. The meaningful change is seeing what people actually do inside the world.
points.concern: First footage does not establish depth, quality, release timing or the terms of any eventual product. This is a creative reveal, not an investment signal.

points.label: The scheduled first look
points.title: A promise that can be checked
points.body: Konami lists the Project ZIRCON session for September 19, 12:15–13:15 in the TGS schedule. The organizer places the show on September 17–21. A session listing is prospective evidence.
points.question: Does the recording deliver actual play?
points.method: Use the official archive and save the exact segment that meets the rule.

points.label: How much was playable?
points.title: Knowledge floor · A minute is a narrow window
points.body: A first demonstration can be polished while the wider experience remains unfinished. Our minimum-duration rule creates a repeatable test, not a quality assessment.
points.question: What can an ordinary player explore beyond the chosen sequence?
points.method: Wait for hands-on access and independent reports. Keep that later assessment separate from this forecast.
